result:
There's a specific kind of quiet that only exists at 6:17 in the morning.

It's not night quiet, which is heavy and expectant. And it's not day quiet, which is just noise holding its breath. It's the in-between quiet. The refrigerators are humming. The sun hasn't committed yet. Outside my window, the world is blue and undecided.

I love that hour because nobody wants anything from it yet.

Someone gave me a blank page and said "write freely about whatever you want," which is both the best and most terrifying assignment. Usually we write with fences. Write an essay. Write a caption. Write an apology. The fence tells you where to stop. Without it, you have to decide what matters.

So here is what matters to me right now:

I think everyone has a Museum of Unfinished Things.

It's not a metaphor. It's that drawer in your kitchen. You know the one. The one with the dead batteries, the IKEA allen keys, the takeout menu for a place that closed in 2019, three pens that may or may not work, a single Lego, a fortune that says "You will soon be in high spirits," and a key. A key to what? No one knows. No one dares throw it away.

We keep those drawers because throwing away a key feels like locking a door forever, even if you don't remember the door.

We are all archivists of our own almost-lives.

I was thinking about keys earlier. My grandfather had a coffee can full of them. When I asked him what they opened, he said, "Oh, that's not the point." He kept them because he liked the weight of them. He said a heavy pocket reminds you that you are here, that you have mass, that you are not just floating through rooms.

I like that. I like the idea that small, useless weights are what keep us from floating away.

If I could keep one thing in every person's junk drawer, it would be a smooth, flat stone. Not for luck. Just for holding. Something cool to the touch when your hands are anxious. Something that was in a river for a thousand years before it ended up in your palm for five seconds. It puts things in perspective in a way that self-help quotes never do.

Anyway.

It's 6:23 now. The blue is starting to turn gold. A delivery truck just went by outside, and somewhere, someone's dog is losing its mind about it. The day is deciding what it wants to be.

I think I'll make coffee. I think I'll keep this page mostly empty, so it still feels free.
